title: John F. Kennedy: 'Ask Not What Your Country Can Do for You' (1961)
summary: On a freezing January morning in 1961, thirty-five-year-old President John F. Kennedy delivered his iconic Inaugural Address, summoning a new generation to civic duty and selfless public service.
keywords: John F. Kennedy: 'Ask Not What Your Country Can Do For You'
full_text:
On a brilliant, freezing morning on January 20, 1961, forty-three-year-old John F. Kennedy stood on the East Front of the Capitol to take the oath of office as the thirty-fifth President of the United States.

Addressing a nation gripped by Cold War anxieties, Kennedy delivered an Inaugural Address of unmatched rhetorical cadence and idealism:

"Let the word go forth from this time and place, to friend and foe alike, that the torch has been passed to a new generation of Americans—born in this century, tempered by war, disciplined by a hard and bitter peace, proud of our ancient heritage...

And so, my fellow Americans:
Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country!
My fellow citizens of the world:
Ask not what America will do for you, but what together we can do for the freedom of man!"

Kennedy’s call to civic responsibility electrified millions of youth, inspiring the creation of the Peace Corps and a renewed commitment to democratic public service worldwide.
